paragraphs: I did a clerkship of about two months at the University of Glasgow in the United Kingdom. Studying abroad in the sixth year had been my goal since I entered the university, and I remember being truly happy when the dispatch to the United Kingdom was decided last year. Clerkships abroad were hard because there were many unfamiliar things, but all the more I was able to have impressive and valuable experiences. Now that my study abroad is over, I would like to introduce the content of the clerkship and the state of life there.

Glasgow is the largest city in Scotland, in the north of the United Kingdom, and since ancient times it was a center of trade and heavy industry that supported the development of the British Empire. Today, while retaining an aspect as an industrial city, it is also known as a city of culture and art. Within the city there are many universities specializing in industry, art, architecture and so on, so many exchange students gather from all over the world. Even when I, an Asian, walked around the city, I did not stand out, so it was very comfortable (although there were no Japanese people at all).

I did my clerkship for six weeks, from 3/25 to 5/3, at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital (QEUH). QEUH is the largest hospital in Scotland and also an educational institution of the University of Glasgow School of Medicine. The wards, just renovated in 2015, were refined in facilities, interior and exterior alike, and I was also surprised by the architectural design, which hardly seemed like a hospital. I was allowed to do clerkships in three clinical departments, centered on Neurology, along with Neurosurgery and Paediatrics.

In Neurology, as in the polyclinic in Japan, I did the clerkship in a group with local students. At 8 in the morning we first received an OSCE lecture, then went to the ward as a group and made rounds of our assigned patients. After that, we observed outpatient clinics and attended bedside teaching and conferences. English conversation in the medical setting was harder than expected, and I felt frustrated many times that English did not come out smoothly, but thanks to the students in the same polyclinic group, who taught me phrases that can be used in examinations and websites for medical students, I was able to get through the clerkship. They also corrected my reports and deciphered the bad handwriting in the charts (some paper charts are still used in the United Kingdom), truly doing everything for me, and I could not thank my polyclinic group mates enough.

Neurosurgery and Paediatrics were departments not originally planned, but when I told my supervising doctor that I was interested in these departments, he willingly permitted me to do clerkships in other departments. Making appointments by an unfamiliar phone was hard, but even with my clumsy English, if I explained properly, the doctors of every department gladly agreed to accept me for the clerkship. In Neurosurgery I was allowed into the surgical field just like the local students. In Paediatrics I was allowed to go not only to QEUH but also to several outside hospitals, and they were very kind, even inviting me to a conference (unfortunately I could not attend because of the schedule).

In this way QEUH, including doctors, staff and students, had an overall very welcoming atmosphere, and if I showed motivation they supported me with all their might. The basic schedule of the clerkship at QEUH is fixed, but it was a very flexible clerkship that can be arranged in any way depending on one's wishes, and I was able to spend truly meaningful time.

For the three weeks from 5/6 to 5/24 I did a clerkship with British family doctors called GPs. In the United Kingdom the primary care system is very well developed, and it is arranged so that GPs are deployed so that there is no maldistribution of doctors in each medical area called a Health Board. The ties among GPs are also strong, and GPs form a community across the whole of Scotland.

This time, with the cooperation of Dr. Logan, a leading figure among the GPs, I asked the GP community to accept an exchange student from Japan. Contrary to my expectation, many GP doctors replied that they would accept me, and I was allowed to do clerkships at six clinics.

In the GP clerkship I mainly observed outpatient clinics and accompanied doctors on home visits. In the outpatient clinic I did not only observe; they prepared a room just for me and let me take histories and examine patients. I had practiced history taking in English with USMLE reference books and the like, but I did not know how to proceed with the history for a chronic-phase patient who had already been diagnosed, and I remember well the awkward silence that passed. At that time what the GP taught me was, "Don't look at the disease, look at the patient as a whole person." When I was shown actual consultations by GPs, I found that history taking and physical examination were kept to the necessary minimum and most of the time was devoted to topics of social aspects such as the patient's employment situation and family relationships. The GP did not ask any special questions, and while chatting frankly with "How have you been lately?", the patients themselves seemed to naturally confide care problems and worries about family relationships. This too is probably the work of the trust relationship with patients that GPs have built over a long time. I was simply moved by the GPs, who could so easily reach the patient's hidden problems that I had not been able to get to.

In addition, in this GP clerkship I was also allowed to do clerkships with a GP working on a remote island and a GP of the child-rearing generation. Even among GPs, each person's way of working differs greatly, which was very interesting.

Since this year was the first time anyone from our university was sent to the University of Glasgow, I felt some tension and anxiety, but thanks to the support of many people I was able to spend a very fulfilling life abroad. I was given the best experience in the last year of my student life. I would like to take this opportunity to thank the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, the staff of QEUH, Dr. 伴信太郎 of general medicine, and the GP doctors.
